records.source: וְאַתָּ֤ה בֶן־אָדָם֙ קַח־לְךָ֣ לְבֵנָ֔ה וְנָתַתָּ֥ה אוֹתָ֖הּ לְפָנֶ֑יךָ וְחַקּוֹתָ֥ עָלֶ֛יהָ עִ֖יר אֶת־יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם׃
records.gloss: And you, son of man, take for yourself a brick and set it before you, and engrave on it a city, Jerusalem.
pieces: "Now, son of man, take a clay brick, set it in front of you, and draw on it a city, Jerusalem.

L.1: "And you, son of man, take for yourself a brick and set it before you, and engrave on it a city, Jerusalem.

R.1: "Son of man, take a clay brick and put it in front of you. Draw a picture of the city of Jerusalem on it.

decisions.choice: the sign-acts: the prophet acts out the message
decisions.reason: Chapters 4-5 are a series of signs that Ezekiel is to act out in front of the exiles: the city under siege (4:1-3), the prophet lying on his side (4:4-8), the starvation rations (4:9-17) and the shaving of his head and beard (5:1-4). Other prophets did the same: Isaiah walked naked and barefoot (Isaiah 20), Jeremiah buried a loincloth, broke a jar and wore a yoke (Jeremiah 13; 19; 27). A sign-act was more than a picture; it announced what the LORD was about to do. Here it portrays the siege of Jerusalem, which began in 588 BC, some five years after Ezekiel's call, and the exile that followed. 5:5-17 explains it.

decisions.choice: a brick ... engrave on it: a clay brick with a drawing scratched into it
decisions.reason: Bricks were made of clay and dried in the sun; while still soft, they could be marked. Babylonian scribes drew plans of buildings and cities on clay. Ezekiel's brick becomes a model of Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: And you: the LORD's speech goes on
decisions.reason: The chapter begins with "And you", carrying on the LORD's words to Ezekiel from 3:24-27. The quotation mark opens again at the chapter break, and the speech runs to the end of verse 12.

decisions.choice: engrave (L); draw (B, R)
decisions.reason: The verb means to cut or scratch a design into a surface. Balanced and Readable say "draw", since the point is the picture of the city. They say "clay brick" so that readers do not picture a fired modern brick.

records.heading: The sign of the siege

records.source: וְנָתַתָּ֨ה עָלֶ֜יהָ מָצ֗וֹר וּבָנִ֤יתָ עָלֶ֨יהָ֙ דָּיֵ֔ק וְשָׁפַכְתָּ֥ עָלֶ֖יהָ סֹֽלְלָ֑ה וְנָתַתָּ֨ה עָלֶ֧יהָ מַחֲנ֛וֹת וְשִׂים־עָלֶ֥יהָ כָּרִ֖ים סָבִֽיב׃
records.gloss: And you will put on it a siege, and build against it a siege wall, and pour out against it a ramp, and set against it camps, and place against it battering rams all around.
pieces: Lay siege to it: build a siege wall against it, heap up a ramp against it, set up army camps around it, and place battering rams against it on every side.

L.2: And you will put a siege against it, and build against it a siege wall, and pour out against it a ramp, and set against it camps, and place against it battering rams all around.

R.2: Then act out an attack on the city. Build siege walls around it, and pile up a dirt ramp against it. Set up army camps, and put battering rams all around it.

decisions.choice: siege wall, ramp, camps and battering rams: the works of a siege army
decisions.reason: These are the methods of ancient siege warfare. The siege wall shut the city in and gave the attackers towers to shoot from (2 Kings 25:1); the ramp was a slope of earth and stones piled against the city wall so that the battering rams could be brought up to it (2 Samuel 20:15; Jeremiah 6:6). Assyrian palace carvings of the siege of Lachish show all of them. Ezekiel is to build a model of them around his brick.

decisions.choice: you will put a siege against it: Ezekiel plays the besieger
decisions.reason: Ezekiel takes the part of the enemy army; verse 3 shows that in doing so he stands for the LORD himself, who is bringing the siege on his own city (5:8).

decisions.choice: act out an attack on the city (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that Ezekiel is acting out the siege with a model. It says "dirt ramp" for the ramp of earth (m1).

records.source: וְאַתָּ֤ה קַח־לְךָ֙ מַחֲבַ֣ת בַּרְזֶ֔ל וְנָתַתָּ֤ה אוֹתָהּ֙ קִ֣יר בַּרְזֶ֔ל בֵּינְךָ֖ וּבֵ֣ין הָעִ֑יר וַהֲכִינֹתָה֩ אֶת־פָּנֶ֨יךָ אֵלֶ֜יהָ וְהָיְתָ֤ה בַמָּצוֹר֙ וְצַרְתָּ֣ עָלֶ֔יהָ א֥וֹת הִ֖יא לְבֵ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃ס
records.gloss: And you, take for yourself a griddle of iron, and you will make it a wall of iron between you and the city, and you will direct your face toward it, and it will be in siege, and you will besiege it; a sign it [is] for [the] house of Israel.
pieces: Then take an iron griddle and set it up as an iron wall between you and the city. Turn to face it. It will be under siege, and you will besiege it. This is a sign for the house of Israel.

L.3: And you, take for yourself an iron griddle, and set it [as] an iron wall between you and the city; and direct your face toward it, and it will be under siege, and you will besiege it. This [is] a sign for the house of Israel.

R.3: Then take an iron baking pan and set it up like an iron wall between you and the city. Turn toward the city. It will be under attack, and you will be the one attacking it. This will be a sign for the people of Israel.

decisions.choice: an iron griddle as an iron wall: a barrier that cannot be broken
alternatives: the barrier between the LORD and the city
decisions.reason: The word is the flat iron plate on which bread was baked (Leviticus 2:5). Set between Ezekiel and the city, it becomes a wall of iron. It may stand for the siege wall that nothing can get through, or for the barrier between the LORD and the city, which he will not lift: Lamentations 3:44 says, "You have covered yourself with a cloud so that no prayer can pass through".

decisions.choice: direct your face toward it: fix your gaze on it in hostility
decisions.reason: The verb means to set or fix; with "face" it means to turn one's whole attention to something. In Ezekiel the face set toward a place is a sign of hostility and judgment (verse 7; 6:2; 13:17; 14:8). See the note at 6:2, where a related phrase is used.

decisions.choice: a sign: an act that shows what is coming
decisions.reason: A sign is something seen that points to something else and guarantees it. Ezekiel's actions are signs of what will happen to Jerusalem (12:6, 11; 24:24, 27); Isaiah's walking naked was a sign in the same way (Isaiah 20:3).

decisions.choice: direct your face toward it (L); turn to face it (B); turn toward (R)
decisions.reason: The verb here, "fix" or "direct", is not the one in the phrase "set your face toward" (6:2), but the sense is close, so Balanced and Readable follow the wording set for that phrase in Ezekiel. Literal says "direct" to keep the two verbs apart. Readable says "baking pan" for the griddle.

records.source: וְאַתָּ֤ה שְׁכַב֙ עַל־צִדְּךָ֣ הַשְּׂמָאלִ֔י וְשַׂמְתָּ֛ אֶת־עֲוֺ֥ן בֵּֽית־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל עָלָ֑יו מִסְפַּ֤ר הַיָּמִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר תִּשְׁכַּ֣ב עָלָ֔יו תִּשָּׂ֖א אֶת־עֲוֺנָֽם׃
records.gloss: And you, lie on your side the left, and put the iniquity of [the] house of Israel on it; [the] number of the days which you lie on it, you will bear their iniquity.
pieces: Then lie on your left side and lay the guilt of the house of Israel on it. For the number of days that you lie on that side, you will bear their guilt.

L.4: And you, lie on your left side, and put the iniquity of the house of Israel upon it; [for] the number of the days that you lie on it, you will bear their iniquity.

R.4: Then lie down on your left side and lay the sin of the people of Israel on yourself. For each day you lie on your side, you will carry the punishment for their sin.

decisions.choice: bear their iniquity: carry the guilt and its punishment
decisions.reason: The word for iniquity means both the wrong and the guilt and punishment that follow it. To "bear iniquity" is to suffer the consequence of sin, as Israel bore its iniquity for forty years in the wilderness, a year for each day (Numbers 14:34). Ezekiel does not take away the people's sin by lying on his side; he acts out the length of their punishment.

decisions.choice: the left side ... the house of Israel: perhaps the northern kingdom
decisions.reason: Facing east, as the Hebrews did to name the directions, the left hand is north and the right hand south. So the left side may stand for the northern kingdom of Israel, and the right side for Judah in the south (verse 6). Elsewhere in Ezekiel "the house of Israel" means the whole people, and it may do so here too.

decisions.choice: lie on your side: for part of each day
decisions.reason: Ezekiel also prepares and eats his food during these days (verses 9-12), so he probably lay on his side for part of each day, in public view, rather than without a break.

decisions.choice: iniquity (L); guilt (B); sin, punishment for sin (R)
decisions.reason: *'Awon* is "iniquity" at Literal, "guilt" or "sin" at Balanced and "sin" at Readable, as in Isaiah. Balanced says "guilt" here because the verse is about bearing it. Readable says "carry the punishment for their sin", which is what bearing iniquity means (m1).

records.heading: Ezekiel lies on his side

records.source: וַאֲנִ֗י נָתַ֤תִּֽי לְךָ֙ אֶת־שְׁנֵ֣י עֲוֺנָ֔ם לְמִסְפַּ֣ר יָמִ֔ים שְׁלֹשׁ־מֵא֥וֹת וְתִשְׁעִ֖ים י֑וֹם וְנָשָׂ֖אתָ עֲוֺ֥ן בֵּֽית־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And I have assigned to you the years of their iniquity to [the] number of days, three hundred and ninety days; and you will bear [the] iniquity of [the] house of Israel.
pieces: I have assigned you a number of days equal to the years of their guilt, 390 days. So you will bear the guilt of the house of Israel.

L.5: And I have assigned to you the years of their iniquity as a number of days, 390 days; and you will bear the iniquity of the house of Israel.

R.5: I have given you one day for each year of their sin: 390 days. For that long you will carry the punishment for the sin of the people of Israel.

decisions.choice: 390 days: the Hebrew number; the Greek translation has 190
decisions.reason: The Hebrew text has 390 days here and in verse 9. The Greek translation reads 190 in both places, and in verse 4 adds that Ezekiel lies on his left side 150 days. Neither number is explained in the text. The 390 years may count from the building of Solomon's temple, or from the division of the kingdom after Solomon, down to the fall of Jerusalem; added to the forty of verse 6, they make 430, the years of Israel in Egypt (Exodus 12:40). The 190 of the Greek may count from the fall of the northern kingdom. The Hebrew number is followed.

decisions.choice: the years ... as a number of days: a day for each year
decisions.reason: Each day Ezekiel lies on his side stands for a year of punishment, as in Numbers 14:34. Verse 6 says so in so many words.

decisions.choice: 390, in numerals (L, B, R)
decisions.reason: Numbers over ninety-nine are written in numerals at every level, as the style guide sets.

records.source: וְכִלִּיתָ֣ אֶת־אֵ֗לֶּה וְשָׁ֨כַבְתָּ֜ עַל־צִדְּךָ֤ הַיְמָנִי֙שֵׁנִ֔ית וְנָשָׂ֖אתָ אֶת־עֲוֺ֣ן בֵּית־יְהוּדָ֑ה אַרְבָּעִ֣ים י֔וֹם י֧וֹם לַשָּׁנָ֛ה י֥וֹם לַשָּׁנָ֖ה נְתַתִּ֥יו לָֽךְ׃
records.gloss: And you will complete these, and you will lie on your side the right a second [time], and you will bear [the] iniquity of [the] house of Judah forty days; a day for the year, a day for the year I have assigned it to you.
pieces: When you have completed these days, lie down again, this time on your right side, and bear the guilt of the house of Judah for forty days. I have assigned you one day for each year.

L.6: And when you have completed these, you will lie down a second [time], on your right side, and you will bear the iniquity of the house of Judah forty days; a day for a year, a day for a year I have assigned it to you.

R.6: When you have finished those days, lie down again, this time on your right side. For forty days you will carry the punishment for the sin of the people of Judah. I have given you one day for each year.

decisions.choice: your right side: the reading tradition
decisions.reason: The written consonants of "right" differ slightly in spelling from the form the scribes' marginal note tells the reader to say. The meaning is the same; the marginal reading is followed.

decisions.choice: forty days, a day for a year: a generation of punishment
decisions.reason: Forty years is the length of a generation, and of Israel's punishment in the wilderness (Numbers 14:33-34). Egypt too is to lie desolate forty years (29:11-13). The number gives Judah's exile the length of a lifetime, not an exact count of years.

decisions.choice: one day for each year (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the repeated "a day for a year, a day for a year". Balanced and Readable say it once, plainly. "Lie down again" gives "a second time".

records.source: וְאֶל־מְצ֤וֹר יְרוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ תָּכִ֣ין פָּנֶ֔יךָ וּֽזְרֹעֲךָ֖ חֲשׂוּפָ֑ה וְנִבֵּאתָ֖ עָלֶֽיהָ׃
records.gloss: And toward the siege of Jerusalem you will direct your face, and your arm [will be] bared, and you will prophesy against it.
pieces: Turn to face the siege of Jerusalem with your arm bared, and prophesy against the city.

L.7: And toward the siege of Jerusalem you will direct your face, with your arm bared, and you will prophesy against it.

R.7: Turn toward Jerusalem, the city under attack. With your arm bare and ready for action, prophesy against it.

decisions.choice: your arm bared: ready to strike
decisions.reason: To bare the arm is to push back the sleeve, ready for action or for battle. Isaiah says that the LORD "has bared his holy arm" before all the nations (Isaiah 52:10). Ezekiel acts out the LORD's power turned against the city.

decisions.choice: you will prophesy against it: words with the sign
decisions.reason: The signs are not silent: Ezekiel is to speak against the city too. His speaking is limited to what the LORD gives him (3:26-27).

decisions.choice: direct your face toward (L); turn to face (B); turn toward (R)
decisions.reason: As in verse 3. Readable says "ready for action" for what the bared arm means (m1).

records.source: וְהִנֵּ֛ה נָתַ֥תִּי עָלֶ֖יךָ עֲבוֹתִ֑ים וְלֹֽא־תֵהָפֵ֤ךְ מִֽצִּדְּךָ֙ אֶל־צִדֶּ֔ךָ עַד־כַּלּוֹתְךָ֖ יְמֵ֥י מְצוּרֶֽךָ׃
records.gloss: And see, I will put on you ropes, and not you will turn from your side to your side until you have completed [the] days of your siege.
pieces: I will tie you up with ropes so that you cannot turn from one side to the other until you have finished the days of your siege.

L.8: And see, I will put cords on you, and you will not turn from your side to your [other] side until you have completed the days of your siege.

R.8: I will tie you up with ropes, so that you cannot turn over from one side to the other until you have finished the days of your attack on the city.

decisions.choice: I will put cords on you: the LORD binds Ezekiel
decisions.reason: Here the LORD himself puts the cords on Ezekiel (compare 3:25). He is held to his task until the days of the sign are complete, as the city will be held in the siege until its end.

decisions.choice: from one side to the other (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "from your side to your side". Balanced and Readable say it as English would. Readable says "your attack on the city" for "your siege", the siege Ezekiel acts out.

records.source: וְאַתָּ֣ה קַח־לְךָ֡ חִטִּ֡ין וּ֠שְׂעֹרִים וּפ֨וֹל וַעֲדָשִׁ֜ים וְדֹ֣חַן וְכֻסְּמִ֗ים וְנָתַתָּ֤ה אוֹתָם֙ בִּכְלִ֣י אֶחָ֔ד וְעָשִׂ֧יתָ אוֹתָ֛ם לְךָ֖ לְלָ֑חֶם מִסְפַּ֨ר הַיָּמִ֜ים אֲשֶׁר־אַתָּ֣ה׀שׁוֹכֵ֣ב עַֽל־צִדְּךָ֗ שְׁלֹשׁ־מֵא֧וֹת וְתִשְׁעִ֛ים י֖וֹם תֹּאכֲלֶֽנּוּ׃
records.gloss: And you, take for yourself wheat and barley and beans and lentils and millet and spelt, and put them in one vessel, and make them for yourself into bread; [the] number of the days which you [are] lying on your side, three hundred and ninety days, you will eat it.
pieces: Take wheat and barley, beans and lentils, millet and spelt. Put them in one container and make bread for yourself from them. You are to eat it during the 390 days that you lie on your side.

L.9: And you, take for yourself wheat and barley and beans and lentils and millet and spelt, and place them in one vessel, and make them into bread for yourself; [for] the number of the days that you are lying on your side, 390 days, you will eat it.

R.9: Take wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet and spelt. Put them all in one bowl and make bread for yourself. Eat it during the 390 days that you lie on your side.

decisions.choice: wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet and spelt: famine bread
decisions.reason: In a siege, when grain runs short, bread is made from whatever is left, mixed together in one jar. Beans and lentils were not normally used for bread. Spelt was a hardy kind of wheat (Exodus 9:32; Isaiah 28:25); the word for millet occurs only here.

decisions.choice: 390 days: as in verse 5
decisions.reason: The Greek translation reads 190 here too. See the note at verse 5. The bread is for the days on the left side; the forty days of verse 6 are not counted here.

decisions.choice: one container (B); one bowl (R)
decisions.reason: The word means any jar or vessel. Readable says "bowl", the picture of mixing; numbers over ninety-nine are in numerals at every level.

records.source: וּמַאֲכָֽלְךָ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר תֹּאכֲלֶ֔נּוּ בְּמִשְׁק֕וֹל עֶשְׂרִ֥ים שֶׁ֖קֶל לַיּ֑וֹם מֵעֵ֥ת עַד־עֵ֖ת תֹּאכֲלֶֽנּוּ׃
records.gloss: And your food which you eat [will be] by weight, twenty shekels for the day; from time to time you will eat it.
pieces: The food you eat is to be weighed out, {{units:about 8 ounces|twenty shekels}} a day, and you are to eat it at set times.

L.10: And your food that you eat [will be] by weight, twenty shekels for the day; from time to time you will eat it.

R.10: You may eat only {{units:about 8 ounces|twenty shekels}} of this bread a day. Eat it at set times.

decisions.choice: twenty shekels a day: a starvation ration
decisions.reason: A shekel was a weight of about two-fifths of an ounce, so twenty shekels was about eight ounces of bread a day, much less than a person needs. Food weighed out by the ounce is a sign of siege famine (verse 16; Leviticus 26:26).

decisions.choice: from time to time: at fixed times
decisions.reason: The phrase means at set intervals, probably once a day. The ration is measured and timed; there is no more.

decisions.choice: about 8 ounces / twenty shekels (units setting)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the shekels. Balanced and Readable give the modern weight, with the shekels as the alternative, as the published books do (ten shekels is about 4 ounces).

records.source: וּמַ֛יִם בִּמְשׂוּרָ֥ה תִשְׁתֶּ֖ה שִׁשִּׁ֣ית הַהִ֑ין מֵעֵ֥ת עַד־עֵ֖ת תִּשְׁתֶּֽה׃
records.gloss: And water by measure you will drink, [the] sixth of the hin; from time to time you will drink.
pieces: You are also to drink water by measure, {{units:about 2/3 quart|a sixth of a hin}}, and drink it at set times.

L.11: And water you will drink by measure, the sixth of a hin; from time to time you will drink [it].

R.11: You may drink only {{units:about 2/3 quart|a sixth of a hin}} of water a day. Drink it at set times.

decisions.choice: a sixth of a hin: about two-thirds of a quart
decisions.reason: A hin was a liquid measure of about a gallon, so a sixth of a hin was about two-thirds of a quart, less than a person needs in a day in a hot climate. Water too will run out in the siege (verse 16).

decisions.choice: about 2/3 quart / a sixth of a hin (units setting)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the hin. Balanced and Readable give the modern measure, with the hin as the alternative, as the published books give a hin as about a gallon. Readable adds "a day", which "from time to time" implies (verse 10).

records.source: וְעֻגַ֥ת שְׂעֹרִ֖ים תֹּֽאכֲלֶ֑נָּה וְהִ֗יא בְּגֶֽלְלֵי֙ צֵאַ֣ת הָֽאָדָ֔ם תְּעֻגֶ֖נָה לְעֵינֵיהֶֽם׃ס
records.gloss: And [as] a cake of barley you will eat it, and it, in dung of excrement of humankind, you will bake it before their eyes.
pieces: Eat it as you would a barley cake, baking it in their sight over dried human dung."

L.12: And [as] a barley cake you will eat it, and you will bake it on dung of human excrement before their eyes."

R.12: Eat the bread as you would eat a flat barley loaf. Bake it while the people watch, using dried human dung as fuel."

decisions.choice: a barley cake baked on human dung: food made unclean
decisions.reason: A barley cake was a round, flat loaf baked on hot stones or embers (1 Kings 19:6). Dried animal dung was a common fuel for such fires, but the Law required human excrement to be buried outside the camp, because the LORD walked in its midst (Deuteronomy 23:13-15). Bread baked over it is unclean. The LORD explains the sign in verse 13.

decisions.choice: before their eyes: in public view
decisions.reason: Like the other signs, this one is done where the exiles can see it.

decisions.choice: dung of human excrement (L); human dung (B, R)
decisions.reason: The words are plain in the Hebrew, and every level keeps them plain, without coarseness and without a softer word that would hide the point (m1). Readable adds "as fuel" to explain the baking. The quotation mark closes the speech that began in 3:24.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֔ה כָּ֣כָה יֹאכְל֧וּ בְנֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל אֶת־לַחְמָ֖ם טָמֵ֑א בַּגּוֹיִ֕ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר אַדִּיחֵ֖ם שָֽׁם׃
records.gloss: And said Yahweh, Thus will eat [the] sons of Israel their bread unclean among the nations where I will drive them there.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} then said, "This is how the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} will eat their food, unclean, among the nations where I will drive them."

L.13: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, "Thus will the sons of Israel eat their bread [as] unclean among the nations, where I will banish them."

R.13: Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} said, "In the same way, the {{gender:Israelites|sons of Israel}} will eat food that is unclean in the foreign lands where I will drive them."

decisions.choice: they will eat their bread unclean among the nations: exile makes everything unclean
decisions.reason: In the land, the people could keep the food laws and bring their offerings to the LORD's house. In a foreign land, away from the temple, their food would be unclean (Hosea 9:3-4; Amos 7:17). The sign of the unclean bread shows the exile as a life cut off from the LORD's presence.

decisions.choice: the Israelites / the sons of Israel (gender setting)
decisions.reason: As at 2:3, Literal keeps "the sons of Israel", and Balanced and Readable say "Israelites" through the gender setting. Readable says "foreign lands" for "the nations".

records.source: וָאֹמַ֗ר אֲהָהּ֙ אֲדֹנָ֣י יְהוִ֔ה הִנֵּ֥ה נַפְשִׁ֖י לֹ֣א מְטֻמָּאָ֑ה וּנְבֵלָ֨ה וּטְרֵפָ֤ה לֹֽא־אָכַ֨לְתִּי֙ מִנְּעוּרַ֣י וְעַד־עַ֔תָּה וְלֹא־בָ֥א בְּפִ֖י בְּשַׂ֥ר פִּגּֽוּל׃ס
records.gloss: And I said, Ah, Lord Yahweh! See, my soul has not been made unclean, and a carcass and a torn [animal] I have not eaten from my youth until now, and not has come into my mouth flesh of foul meat.
pieces: Then I said, "Oh, Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}}! I have never made myself unclean. From my youth until now I have never eaten anything that died by itself or was torn by wild animals, and no spoiled sacrificial meat has ever entered my mouth."

L.14: And I said, "Ah, Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}}! See, my soul has not been made unclean; and what dies [of itself] and what is torn I have not eaten from my youth until now, and no foul meat has come into my mouth."

R.14: Then I said, "Oh no, Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}}! I have never made myself unclean. Since I was young, I have never eaten meat from an animal that died by itself or was killed by wild animals. I have never put any unclean meat in my mouth."

decisions.choice: what dies of itself, what is torn, foul meat: the meat the Law forbids
decisions.reason: The Law forbids eating an animal that has died by itself or been killed by wild animals (Exodus 22:30; Leviticus 17:15), and priests most of all (Leviticus 22:8; Ezekiel 44:31). "Foul meat" is the meat of a sacrifice left too long, which had become unclean (Leviticus 7:18; 19:7). Ezekiel the priest has kept himself clean all his life.

decisions.choice: Ah, Lord GOD! my soul has not been made unclean: Ezekiel's only protest
decisions.reason: This is the one place where Ezekiel objects to a command. Peter's protest in Acts 10:14, "I have never eaten anything common or unclean", is much like it.

decisions.choice: Ah, Lord GOD (L); Oh, Lord GOD (B); Oh no, Lord GOD (R)
decisions.reason: The cry is worded as Jeremiah 1:6. Balanced and Readable say "myself" for "my soul", which here means the whole person, and "spoiled sacrificial meat" (B) and "unclean meat" (R) for "foul meat" (m1).

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלַ֔י רְאֵ֗ה נָתַ֤תִּֽי לְךָ֙ אֶת־צְפִיעֵ֣י הַבָּקָ֔ר תַּ֖חַת גֶּלְלֵ֣י הָֽאָדָ֑ם וְעָשִׂ֥יתָ אֶֽת־לַחְמְךָ֖ עֲלֵיהֶֽם׃ס
records.gloss: And he said to me, See, I give to you [the] dung of the cattle in place of [the] dung of humankind, and you will make your bread on them.
pieces: He said to me, "Very well, I will let you use cow dung instead of human dung. You may bake your bread over that."

L.15: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to me, "See, I give you cow dung in place of human dung, and you will make your bread on it."

R.15: He answered, "All right. I will let you use cow dung instead of human dung to bake your bread."

decisions.choice: dung: the reading tradition
decisions.reason: The written consonants of the word for dung differ slightly in spelling from the form the scribes' marginal note gives. The meaning is the same.

decisions.choice: I give you cow dung in place of human dung: the LORD hears his servant
decisions.reason: The LORD changes the sign at Ezekiel's request. The point of the sign, that the exiles' food will be unclean, still stands; but the LORD listens to the prophet's objection, as he listens to Abraham and Moses (Genesis 18:22-33; Exodus 32:11-14).

decisions.choice: Very well (B); All right (R)
decisions.reason: The pointing word, traditionally "behold", here marks a concession. Literal says "See"; Balanced and Readable give the sense of the reply.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלַ֗י בֶּן־אָדָם֙ הִנְנִ֨י שֹׁבֵ֤ר מַטֵּה־לֶ֨חֶם֙ בִּיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם וְאָכְלוּ־לֶ֥חֶם בְּמִשְׁקָ֖ל וּבִדְאָגָ֑ה וּמַ֕יִם בִּמְשׂוּרָ֥ה וּבְשִׁמָּמ֖וֹן יִשְׁתּֽוּ׃
records.gloss: And he said to me, Son of man, see, I [am] breaking [the] staff of bread in Jerusalem, and they will eat bread by weight and with anxiety, and water by measure and with horror they will drink,
pieces: He also said to me, "Son of man, I am about to break the staff of bread in Jerusalem. They will eat bread weighed out with anxiety and drink water measured out in despair,

L.16: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to me, "Son of man, see, I am breaking the staff of bread in Jerusalem, and they will eat bread by weight and with anxiety, and they will drink water by measure and with horror,

R.16: He said to me, "Son of man, I am going to take away the food supply in Jerusalem. The people will weigh out their bread and eat it with worry. They will measure out their water and drink it in fear.

decisions.choice: I am breaking the staff of bread ... bread by weight: the curse of Leviticus 26:26
decisions.reason: Bread is the staff that supports life. Leviticus 26:26 warns that if Israel breaks the covenant, the LORD will "break the staff of bread", and bread will be handed out by weight. Ezekiel's rations in verses 10-11 act out this curse, and the same phrase returns in 5:16 and 14:13. Much of chapters 4-5 echoes Leviticus 26.

decisions.choice: with anxiety ... with horror: the fear of starvation
decisions.reason: The two words describe the mood of a starving city: worry over every mouthful, and dismay as the food and water run out.

decisions.choice: break the staff of bread (L, B); take away the food supply (R)
decisions.reason: As in Leviticus 26:26. The verse runs on into verse 17 at Literal and Balanced.

records.source: לְמַ֥עַן יַחְסְר֖וּ לֶ֣חֶם וָמָ֑יִם וְנָשַׁ֨מּוּ֙ אִ֣ישׁ וְאָחִ֔יו וְנָמַ֖קּוּ בַּעֲוֺנָֽם׃פ
records.gloss: so that they will lack bread and water, and they will be appalled a man and his brother, and they will rot away in their iniquity.
pieces: so that they will run short of bread and water. They will look at one another in horror and waste away under their guilt."

L.17: so that they will lack bread and water, and they will be appalled, each with his brother, and they will rot away in their iniquity."

R.17: They will run out of food and water. They will stare at one another in shock, and they will waste away because of their sin."

decisions.choice: they will rot away in their iniquity: Leviticus 26:39
decisions.reason: Leviticus 26:39 says that the survivors in the lands of their enemies "will rot away in their iniquity". The phrase is used again in 24:23 and 33:10. It pictures people wasting away under the weight of their guilt and its punishment.

decisions.choice: a man and his brother: one another
decisions.reason: The idiom means "one another": everyone looks at everyone else, appalled.

decisions.choice: waste away under their guilt (B)
decisions.reason: Balanced follows Leviticus 26:39 in saying "waste away". The quotation mark closes at the chapter break; the speech goes on in chapter 5.
